chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ammar ibn al-Mubarak, from Muhammad ibn Uthayfir, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I rise [for prayer] when the dawn has broken, and I have not yet prayed the night prayer.' He said: 'Pray the night prayer, and pray the odd [witr], and pray the two rak'ahs of dawn.'

Thus, these narrations came as a concession (rukhsah) permitting the delay of the morning prayer from the beginning of its time to its end. This is permissible if the delay is solely for engaging in some act of worship. The preferable method is what we mentioned: that one prays the morning prayer at the beginning of its time, then makes up the night prayer. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is [this principle].

key_terms.رَكْعَتَا الْفَجْرِ: The two rak'ahs of dawn prayer
key_terms.رُخْصَةً: A concession or dispensation in Islamic law
key_terms.لِلِاشْتِغَالِ بِشَيْءٍ مِنَ الْعِبَادَا: For engaging in acts of worship

ai.seo_question: What is the correct order of prayers if one wakes up after sunrise and missed the night prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic nuance of delaying the Fajr prayer to prioritize night worship (Tahajjud), establishing it as a permissible concession (rukhsa) rather than a neglect of duty. The Imam’s instruction to pray Tahajjud, Witr, and then Fajr sunnah highlights the hierarchical value of voluntary night prayers in Shia spirituality, while the commentary emphasizes that the optimal practice remains performing the obligatory Fajr at its earliest time before engaging in additional worship.
